name: EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery)
seoTitle: EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery): work out your last period from the LMP EDD and the ultrasound weeks. A free health calculator with the formula, units…
summary: your last period is what the EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) calculator works out, and it gets there from the LMP EDD, the ultrasound weeks, the ultrasound days and the ultrasound EDD. It is built for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) calculator work?
sections.html:
The EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports your last period in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the menstrual cycle length); then you give the LMP EDD and the ultrasound EDD; then you type in the ultrasound weeks, the ultrasound days and the difference.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Your last period=LMP EDD − 281
Date of the ultrasound=ultrasound days + 7 × ultrasound weeks + ultrasound EDD − menstrual cycle length − 281
Current date=ultrasound (US) age + ultrasound EDD − 281
Current date=last Menstrual Period (LMP) age + LMP EDD − 281
Ultrasound (US) age=last Menstrual Period (LMP) age + difference

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in weeks / days
  • Time, opening in weeks / days

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the LMP EDD, the ultrasound weeks and the ultrasound days — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns your last period, derived from the LMP EDD, the ultrasound weeks and the ultrasound days. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the LMP EDD, the ultrasound weeks, the ultrasound days and the ultrasound EDD, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter last Menstrual Period (LMP) age in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Last Menstrual Period (LMP) age opens in weeks / days and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the EDD (Estimated Date of Delivery) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
